newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Moslems mark haj climax after 217 die in fire.
newsitem.headline: Moslems mark haj climax after 217 die in fire.

text.p: Saudi authorities tried on Wednesday to identify more than 200 victims of a fire that swept their tent city, as two million Moslems began the climax of this year's ill-fated haj pilgrimage.
Saudi Arabia said the fire, fanned by high winds, had killed 217 people and injured another 1,290. There was no breakdown of victims' nationalities.

But diplomats and Saudi authorities awaited higher casualty figures from the blaze, which had spread panic among thousands of pilgrims performing Islam's holiest duty and engulfed 70,000 white tents in the Mena plain, 11 km (seven miles) from Mecca.

"All our efforts to get an idea of the number of dead are in vain. Hospital staff are not authorised to speak and the Saudi authorities are not sharing new information with the embassies or press," a diplomat said.
While the search of the charred debris continued, swarms of white-robed pilgrims by midday Wednesday had reached Mount Arafat, pinnacle of an elaborate set of haj rituals.
Other Moslems -- chanting "I have answered your call, God, there is no God but you" -- made their way there slowly under a sea of multi-coloured umbrellas.
Diplomats and witnesses said Tuesday's blaze was caused by gas cylinder explosions but Riyadh gave no cause.

In Mena, the air was thick with the smell of smoke and the ground was littered with remains from burnt-out buses to charred water bottles. Trucks carted off blackened debris, while workers -- helped by the Saudi army -- frantically erected new tents.
Some pilgrims gave up on achieving one of the five tenets of Islam this year.
"We will come next year for haj, because we have lost everything," one Pakistani pilgrim told Reuters of his group of 10 who were turning back to Mecca.
Diplomats said Saudi authorities were trying to identify victims, a difficult task as many bodies were thoroughly burnt.

"We do not have new casualty figures. We expect they will run into three figures," said Indian Ambassador Mohammad Hamad Ansari. "It's hard to say because the bodies were charred in the fire and we cannot identify them except from a missing persons list."
"It could be 100, it could be more," he said of the number of Indian victims, which on Tuesday he put at 100.
Diplomats had said most victims were from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Saudi newspapers said the fire had also engulfed Syrian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni and Moroccan tents.
In Pakistan, the Foreign Ministry said 12 of at least 30 Pakistanis killed had been identified. Pakistan haj official Aftab Zaidi said Pakistani victims would be buried in Saudi Arabia.

Praying at Mount Arafat, where Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago, marks the climax of haj. On Thursday, Moslems around the world celebrate Eid al-Adha (Feast of Sacrifice) at the end of haj.
Pilgrims will spend the night at Mozdalifah, between Mena and Mount Arafat, where they will stone three pillars symbolising the devil.
Newspapers said many pilgrims had not yet reached the tents when the fire broke out, preventing more loss of life.

Saudi Health Minister Osama bin Abdul-Majid Shobokshi said on Saudi television on Wednesday the response of civil defence and fire fighters also had saved many lives. "Many of the injured are in satisfactory condition. Many of them have already left hospitals," he said.

King Fahd expressed condolences to the families of the victims. Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said he was deeply aggrieved and U.S. President Bill Clinton said in Washington he was deeply saddened.

The blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca, Islam's holiest shrine. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to make the haj at least once if they can afford it. In 1990 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a stampede in a tunnel and in 1994 270 pilgrims died in another stampede.
Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion in the last decade on expanding pilgrimage sites and officials had vowed to ensure a safe haj.
